question.problem:
For the function $f:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R,$ defined as

$$
f\left(x,y \right) 
=
x^2y-xy^3,
$$

determine the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14134795/assets/0de380d24ed675cff86b219a2a4a337699d68e168fc875475158523022915b0c.svg) Give your answer in matrix form.
question.worked_solution:
Suppose that the function $\mathbf{f}:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ is defined by 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14134795/assets/61c5a4204c4ad078bd036eee7770e28faf4741bedb274a54d08d54dae43fbc68.svg) 

and is twice differentiable at $\mathbf x = \mathbf a.$ Then, the quadratic Taylor polynomial of $f$ about $\mathbf a$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & ≈f(a)+{f}^{′}(a)(x-a)+\frac{1}{2}(x-a)^{T}{f}^{″}(a)(x-a),\end{aligned}
$$

where

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14134795/assets/ab531b6a5468a0ddb8cf46a42300f19cc6406c94c011ae814d60af24f66e2aa0.svg)

and

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14134795/assets/3dbb0d517f6875d4a0601ba284878cb60ac0b615491564ae9458c34c0f3de403.svg)

In this case, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & \frac{∂f}{∂y}\end{aligned}], & \,{f}^{″}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{x}^{2}} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂x∂y} \\ \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂y∂x} & \frac{{∂}^{2}f}{∂{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we compute the terms of our Taylor polynomial:

- Calculating the value of the function, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1,1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the first derivatives, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}2xy-{y}^{3} & {x}^{2}-3x{y}^{2}\end{aligned}] \\ {f}^{′}(1,1) & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

- Calculating the second derivative, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{″}(x) & =[\begin{aligned}2y & 2x-3{y}^{2} \\ 2x-3{y}^{2} & -6xy\end{aligned}] \\ {f}^{″}(1,1) & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ -1 & -6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the second-degree Taylor polynomial (in matrix form) is given by

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14134795/assets/3cbbec95c6327e77a53bdeea5de4a93481ca9f4164ebae0cb99bf28468513a12.svg)
